I.

Introduction

[
1
]

The Attorney General of Canada (“AGC”), applies
to strike the petitioner’s amended petition filed April 24, 2023 (“Petition”), without
leave to amend.

[
2
]

The petitioner, The Friends of Fairy Creek
Society (“Society”), seeks the following order in the Petition:

An order
declaring that the
Migratory
Birds Act Regulations 2022
(SOR/2022) [
sic
] prohibit the indescriminate
[
sic
] destruction of Marbled Murrelet nests by the logging of old growth
trees in
TFL 46 [a tree forest licence area located on southern Vancouver Island].

[
3
]

By separate application, the Attorney General of
British Columbia and Minister of Forests (“AGBC”) also apply to strike the Petition,
without leave to amend, and dismiss the proceeding.

[
4
]

I will address both the AGC and AGBC
applications as they both seek the same relief, which is to strike the Petition
pursuant to Rule 9-5(1) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg.
168/2009 [
SCCR
].

[
5
]

The AGC relies on Rule 9-5(1), grounds (a) - it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be; (b) - it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious; and (d) - it is otherwise an
abuse of the process of the court.

[
6
]

The AGBC relies on ground (a), and in oral
submissions at the hearing of these applications the AGBC agreed with and
adopted the submissions of the AGC.

II.

Background

[
7
]

The purpose of the Society is stated in the
Petition to be “to preserve the remaining old growth forests in the area
designated in Tree Farm Licence 46.”

[
8
]

The factual basis of the Petition is summarized
as follows:

1.

The marbled murrelet is a small seabird of the
North Pacific that nest in old growth forest. The bird is a “protected species”
under the
MBCA
, and is designated as a “threatened species” under the

federal
Species at Risk Act
, S.C. 2002, c. 29 [
SARA
], and the
provincial
Forest and Range Practices Act
, S.B.C. 2002, c. 69.

2.

TFL 46 is a block of forest on southern
Vancouver Island. Teal Cedar is a British Columbia company provincially
authorized to engage in logging and other associated rights in TFL 46.

3.

Old growth trees have been harvested in TFL 46,
including areas estimated to be suitable for marbled murrelet habitat.

4.

Continued logging of old growth trees in TFL 46
will negatively impact nesting opportunities for marbled murrelets, and the
loss of nests.

[
9
]

The legal basis of the Petition refers to Rule 2-1(2)(c)
of the
SCCR
, which requires the filing of a petition where:

the sole or
principal question at issue is alleged to be one of construction of an
enactment …

[
10
]

Here, the enactment referred to in the Petition is
s. 5 of the
MBR
, as follows:

Prohibitions

5
(1)
A person
must not engage in any of the following activities unless they have a permit
that authorizes them to do so or they are authorized by these Regulations to do
so:

(a)

capture, kill, take, injure or harass a migratory
bird or attempt to do so;

(b)   destroy,
take or disturb an egg; and

(c)

damage,
destroy, remove or disturb a nest, nest shelter, eider duck shelter or duck
box.

Exceptions

(2)

However
, the
following
may be
damaged, destroyed, removed or disturbed without a permit:

(a)

a nest shelter, eider duck shelter or duck box that does not
contain a live bird or a viable egg;

(b)

a nest that was built by a species that is not listed in a Table
to Schedule 1 if that nest does not contain a live bird or a viable egg; and

(c)

a nest that was built by a species that is listed in a Table to
Schedule 1 if the following conditions are met:

(i)

the
person who damages, destroys, removes or disturbs that nest provided a written
notice to the Minister a number of months beforehand that corresponds to the
number of months set out in column 3 of the relevant Table to that Schedule for
the species, and

(ii)

the
nest has not been used by migratory birds since the notice was received by the
Minister.

III.

Parties’ Positions

Position of the AGC and AGBC

[
11
]

The AGC applies to strike out the Petition pursuant
to Rule 9-5(1)(d), abuse of process, also relying on grounds (a) and (b):

9-5
(1)  At any stage of a proceeding, the court may order to be struck out or amended
the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)

it discloses no
reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)

it is unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)

…

(d)

it is otherwise an
abuse of the process of the court,

and
the court may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or
dismissed and may order the costs of the application to be paid as special
costs.

[
12
]

Rule 9-5(2) provides that no evidence is admissible on an
application under Ruel 9-5(1)(a), but may be considered on an application under
the remaining paragraphs of Rule 9-5(1).

Rule 9-5(1)(a): it discloses no reasonable claim or defence

[
13
]

A summary of the AGC’s submissions on Rule 9-5(1)(a) is that the
Petition:

1.

does not disclose the type of claim that may be brought by way of
petition, and does not seek any enforceable relief, recourse, or remedy as
against Canada or anyone;

2.

impugns no action or inaction on the part of Canada or anyone;

3.

challenges no federal legislation nor any provincial legislation;

4.

if granted would settle no live controversy between the parties.

[
14
]

The AGBC supports and adopts the submissions of the AGC, and in the
AGBC’s own application seeks an order striking the Petition on the ground it is
an abuse of process.

[
15
]

The AGBC submits that it is plain and obvious the Petition cannot
succeed as a matter of law because it amounts to an abstract legal opinion that
will not have any practical utility in any live controversy between the
parties, which cannot be cured by amendment.

Rule 9-5(1)(b): it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious

[
16
]

The AGC also refers to Rule 9-5(1)(b), submitting that the Petition
is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, and the granting of the
declaration will have no practical effect on Canada or the Society.

[
17
]

The AGC submits that the wording of the Petition suggests it seeks a
finding of this Court to enlist Canada in the petitioner’s efforts to halt
logging in TFL 46, which is akin to an order for
mandamus
against Canada
falling within the jurisdiction of the Federal Court of Canada pursuant to

ss. 17
and
18
of the
Federal Courts Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7 [
FCA
].

[
18
]

As a result, the AGC submits that the lack of clarity in the
pleading precludes a determination as to whether this Court has proper
jurisdiction or whether the matter is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the
Federal Court of Canada, citing
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
, at para.
20
,
where Justice Fisher notes that “… if a pleading is so confusing that it is
difficult to understand what is pleaded, it may also be unnecessary, frivolous
or vexatious.”

Rule
9-5(1)(d): it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court

[
19
]

The AGC emphasizes Rule 9-5(1)(d), submitting that the Petition is
an abuse of process because it attempts to enforce legislation that involves
penal consequences if breached. The AGC’s submissions are summarized as
follows:

1.

The declaration sought by the petitioner is that the
MBR
prohibit
the indiscriminate destruction of marbled murrelet nests by the logging of old
growth forests in TFL 46;

2.

Contravening s. 5(1) of the
MBR
constitutes an “offence”
under s. 13(1) of the
MBCA
; and s. 13(2)-(4) of the
MBCA

imposes penalties for offences committed under s. 13(1) of the
MBCA
.
These offences can be based on either a conviction on indictment or summary
conviction;

3.

The petitioner, a private society, may not use the court to enforce
the offences and penalties under the
MBR
and
MBCA;
the Petition
constitutes an abuse of process as a colourable attempt to enforce criminal
sanctions privately.

[
20
]

The AGC cites
Reece v. Edmonton (City)
,
2010 ABQB 538
;
Reece
v. Edmonton (City),
2011 ABCA 238
; and
R. v. Shore Disposal
,
1976 CanLII 1235 (NS CA)
, [1976]
N.S.J. No. 404, 16 N.S.R.(2d) 538 (C.A.) in support of the AGC’s
submission that seeking a declaration to enforce or engage punitive penal
statutes is an abuse of process.

Position of Teal Cedar

[
21
]

Teal Cedar is not named as a respondent in the Petition, but did file
a response to the Petition, opposing the orders sought by the Society.

[
22
]

Teal Cedar did not file an application response to either
application of the AGC and AGBC. The application record includes a letter from
Teal Cedar’s counsel to AGC and AGBC’s counsel consenting to the AGC and AGBC’s
applications to strike the Petition for the reasons set out in Teal Cedar’s
response to the Petition, which are that the Petition is an abuse of process,
is bound to fail, and should be struck under Rule 9-5.

Position of The Friends of Fairy
Creek Society

[
23
]

The Society’s opposition to the applicants’ applications is that it
is not plain and obvious that the claim cannot succeed; the ruling requested by
the Society would have practical utility; and the ruling would made a tangible
difference to the rights of the parties.

[
24
]

The Petition poses the question before the Court as being not
whether logging in TFL 46 is lawful, but only the narrow question of whether
such logging is exempted from the prohibitions contained in the
MBR
.

IV.

Legal Framework

[
25
]

The following is a summary of the legal principles applicable to a
consideration of the AGC and AGBC applications seeking to strike the Petition
pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d).

Rule 9-5(1)(a): it discloses no
reasonable claim or defence

[
26
]

Rule 9-5(1)(a) provides that the court may order a petition struck
out on the ground that it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case
may be.

[
27
]

The test for striking a pleading under Rule
9-5(1)(a) was set out in
Union Road Properties Ltd. v. British Columbia (Agricultural
Land Commission)
,
2019 BCCA 302
at para.
9
, quoting
Willow,
as
follows:

[18]      The
test for striking a claim as disclosing no reasonable claim under rule
9-5(1)(a), set out in
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII
90 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 SCR 959
and reiterated more recently in
R. v.
Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd
.,
2011 SCC 42
,
is whether it is “plain
and obvious,” assuming the facts pleaded are true, that the claim discloses no
reasonable cause of action, has no reasonable prospect of success, or if the
action is “certain to fail
.” If there is a chance that the plaintiffs might
succeed, then they should not be “driven from the judgment seat.” No evidence
is admissible on an application under rule 9-5 (1)(a).

[Emphasis
added.]

[
28
]

The test is somewhat modified when the
application is to strike a petition rather than a notice of civil claim. In
E.
B. v. Director of Child, Family and Community Services
,
2016 BCCA 66
at para.
42
,
the Court of Appeal for British Columbia stated:

…
A petition need not disclose a “cause of action”, but must set out a foundation
for a type of proceeding authorized to be brought by petition. Accordingly, the
correct inquiry under Rule 9-5(1)(a) in this case is whether the petition
disclosed the type of claim that may be brought by petition.

[
29
]

Rule 9-5(2) provides that no evidence is
admissible on an application under Rule 9-5(1)(a). Material facts in the claim
must be taken as true, explained in
Simon v. Canada (Attorney General)
,

2015 BCSC 924
at para.
55
quoting
Gill v. Canada
,
2013 BCSC 1703
as
follows:

[7]        Rule 9-5(2) stipulates that no
evidence is admissible in the context of an application under Rule 9-5(1)(a).
Another way of putting this stipulation is that the court should assume that
the facts [pleaded are] true as it considers whether those facts disclose a
reasonable claim. A common sense exception to this stipulation exists when the
pleadings assert some bizarre or impossible proposition.
The
purpose of Rule 9-5(1)(a) is to ensure that the parties and the court have a
clear understanding of the nature of the claims advanced
.
A clear
understanding of the claims will allow the parties to efficiently litigate the
issues and will allow the court to make considered and judicious findings on
those issues
.
Prolix, convoluted, and incomprehensible pleadings do not
lend themselves to permit in the parties to achieve a clear understanding of
the claims advanced. Further, a party pleading a particular type of claim must,
at a minimum, plead assertions of fact which, if proven, would establish the
essential elements of a successful claim.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
30
]

Here, the petitioner’s claim is for an order for a declaration that
the
MBR
prohibit the indiscriminate destruction of marbled murrelet
nests by the logging of old growth trees in TFL 46.

[
31
]

The following is a summary of legal principles regarding declaratory
relief:

1.

Declaratory relief is a discretionary remedy that “may be
appropriate where (a) the court has jurisdiction to hear the issue, (b) the
dispute is real and not theoretical, (c) the party raising the issue has a
genuine interest in its resolution, and (d) the responding party has an
interest in opposing the declaration being sought”:
Interfor Corporation v.
Mackenzie Sawmill Ltd.,

2022 BCCA 228
at para.
25
, referring to
S.A.
v. Metro Vancouver Housing Corp
.,
2019 SCC 4
at para.
60
.

2.

In addition, a declaration must have practical utility, in that it
will settle a “live controversy” between the parties or clarify the rights of
the parties, at least to some extent:
Daniels v. Canada (Indian Affairs and
Northern Development)
,
2016 SCC 12
at para.
11
;
West
Moberly First Nations v. British Columbia
,
2020 BCCA 138
at paras.
308–314
,
331, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, [2020] S.C.C.A. No. 252.

3.

A declaration is not a mere observation or comment
by the court on how it views a situation. Rather, it is a binding statement by
the court establishing a right, power, duty or status.
A declaration is a discretionary remedy. Even if a person
establishes the existence of a right, power, duty or status, a court will
generally not grant the remedy unless it considers that it will have practical
effect and resolve an extant legal dispute
: Pereira
v. British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board
),

2023 BCCA 195
at para.
16
.

4.

Generally, modern courts have continued to adhere to the principle
that declaratory actions should not be entertained where the declaration will
serve little or no practical purpose or raises a matter of only hypothetical
interest. Conversely, where the pleadings disclose a “real difficulty,” present
or threatened, the action will lie:

Pereira
at para.
18
, quoting
Cheslatta Carrier Nation v. British Columbia
,
2000
BCCA 539
at para.
13
.

5.

A declaration constitutes a formal and binding statement
establishing the existence of a right, power, duty or status. It is not a mere
observation by the court, nor is it a form of admonition to an administrative
body:

Pereira
at para.
23
.

[
32
]

The practical utility consideration was
discussed in more detail in
West Moberly
in the majority reasons of
Chief Justice Bauman, as follows:

[311]    This Court has
also phrased the question as “whether a ‘useful purpose’ would be served by
granting the order”:
Wakelam v. Wyeth Consumer Healthcare/Wyeth Soins
de Sante Inc.
,
2014 BCCA 36
at para.
71
; see also
Greater
Vancouver Regional District v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2011
BCCA 345
at para.
52
[
GVRD
].

[312]    An assessment of
the practical utility of a declaration necessarily looks at the effect of the
requested remedy on the parties’ rights. Declarations must be connected to
legal rights, rather than, for example, facts “detached” from those rights or
“law generally”:
1472292 Ontario Inc. (Rosen Express) v. Northbridge
General Insurance Company
,
2019 ONCA 753
at para.
30
;
Gouriet
v. Union of Post Office Workers
,
[1978] A.C. 435
at 501
. Detached facts and general pronouncements of law have little
utility.

…[Heading
omitted.]

[313]    For a
declaration to have practical utility, thus, it must “define” some aspect of
the parties’ rights: Reasons of Justice Smith at para. 69.

[314]    The question for
the court is “whether the declaration is
capable of having any
practical effect
in resolving the issues in the case”:
Solosky
at 833
(emphasis added). In other words, declarations will only be certain to lack
practical utility where it is clear the declaration sought will have
no
effect
.

[Emphasis in
original.]

Rule 9-5(1)(b):
it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious

[
33
]

Rule 9-5(1)(b) provides that the court may order to be struck out or
amended the whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document on the
ground that it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious.

[
34
]

I
n
Willow
, Fisher J. explained that
under Rule 9-5(1)(b):

[20]      …
a pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if
it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause of action, if it does not
advance any claim known in law, where it is obvious that an action cannot
succeed, or where it would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste of the
court's time and public resources
:
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
[1999] BCJ No. 2160
(SC)
;
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
.
If a
pleading is so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, it
may also be unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious. An application under this
sub-rule may be supported by evidence.

[
35
]

Justice

Fisher’s quote was cited with approval in
Nevsun
Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,
2020 SCC 5
at para.
65
.

Rule 9-5(1)(d):
it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court

[
36
]

The court’s discretion to order the whole or any
part of a pleading, petition or other document to be struck under Rule
9-5(1)(d) is broad and flexible, as explained in
Willow

by Fisher J., as
follows:

[21]      Abuse of process
under Rule 9-5(1)(d) or the court’s inherent discretion is a flexible doctrine.

It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would
violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity
of the administration of justice
. A claim may be struck where it is a
collateral attack on an administrative decision that is subject to appeal or
judicial review: [citations omitted].

[22]      The
plaintiffs have an obligation to clearly
plead the
material facts upon which they rely in making their claim. A material fact is a
fact that is essential in formulating a complete cause of action: see
Young
at
para. 20 [
Young v Borzoni
,
2007 BCCA 16
].

[23]      In
considering an application to strike under Rule 9-5, the court should consider
whether defective pleadings can be corrected by way of an amendment and whether
it would be appropriate to give leave to do so: see
Greville v Convoy
Supply Ltd.
(14 January 2004), Vancouver S033090 (BCSC)

[Emphasis
added.]

[
37
]

In
Babavic v. Babowech
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802,
42 A.C.W.S. (3d) 447
Justice Baker considered the scope of abuse of process in
relation to the predecessor to Rule 9-5, as follows:

17.
Rule
19(24) is a
codification
of the court's inherent jurisdiction to stay actions
that are an
abuse of process or that disclose no reasonable cause of
action:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.

(1990),
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
,
74 D.L.R. (4th) 321
at 327 (S.C.C.)
. The
principle of abuse of process is somewhat amorphous.
The discretion afforded
courts to dismiss actions on the ground of abuse of process extends
to any circumstance in which the court process is used
for an improper purpose
. I.H. Jacob, in
"The Inherent Jurisdiction of the Court", (1970) Current Legal
Problems 23 at pp.40-41 provides the following definition of this principle:

"
It connotes that the process
of the court must be used properly, honestly and in good faith, and must not be
abused. It means that the court will not allow its function as a court of law
to be misused
, and it will summarily prevent its machinery from being used
as a means of vexation or oppression in the process of litigation. Unless the
court had power to intervene summarily to prevent the misuse of legal
machinery, the nature and function of the court would be transformed from a
court dispensing justice into an instrument of injustice.

It follows that where an abuse of
process has taken place, the intervention of the court by stay or even
dismissal of proceedings may often be required by the very essence of justice
to be done
, and so to prevent parties
being harassed and put to expense by frivolous, vexatious or groundless
litigation."

18.
The
categories of abuse of process are open. Abuse of process may be found where
proceedings involve a deception on the court or constitute a mere sham; where the
process of the court is not
being
fairly or
honestly used, or is employed for some ulterior or improper purpose;
proceedings which are without foundation or serve no useful purpose and
multiple or successive proceedings which cause or are likely to cause vexation
or oppression. These are discussed by Jacob, supra, at p. 43 of his
article.

[Emphasis added.
]

V.

Judicial Notice

[
38
]

The Society invites the Court to take judicial notice of a number of
statements, summarized as follows: (1) the logging of old-growth forests in TFL
46 has been the subject of significant controversy and litigation over the last
three years, involving litigation including injunction applications, contempt
proceedings, small claims court matters, complaints regarding RCMP conduct, and
a civil claim for conspiracy; (2) the litigation involves Teal Cedar, the AGC
and AGBC, both of whom support Teal Cedar’s right to log old-growth trees, and
the AGC and the AGBC have supported the prosecution of protestors; (3) the
dispute over old-growth logging in Fairy Creek has resulted in the largest
number of arrests for civil disobedience in Canadian history; (4) the question
of whether Teal Cedar’s logging of old-growth in TFL 46 is in compliance with
the
MBR
is a critical part of a significant public dispute.

[
39
]

In
R. v. Find
,
2001 SCC 32
, the Supreme
Court of Canada explained the meaning of judicial notice:

[48]           …
Judicial notice dispenses with the need for proof of facts that are clearly
uncontroversial or beyond reasonable dispute. Facts judicially noticed are not
proved by evidence under oath. Nor are they tested by cross-examination. Therefore,
the  threshold for judicial notice is strict: a court may properly take
judicial notice of facts that are either: (1) so notorious or generally
accepted as not to be the subject of debate among reasonable persons; or (2)
capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to readily accessible
sources of indisputable accuracy:
R. v. Potts
(1982),
1982
CanLII 1751 (ON CA)
,
66 C.C.C. (2d) 219 (Ont. C.A.)
; J. Sopinka, S. N. Lederman
and A. W. Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada
(2nd ed.
1999), at p. 1055.

[
40
]

T
aking judicial notice of a fact when it is inappropriate to
do so is an error of law:
see
R. v. Poperechny
,
2020 MBCA 81
at para.
27
.

[
41
]

In
R. v. R.M.,
2023 BCCA 455
,
the Court of Appeal for British Columbia referred
to circumstances where the standard for judicial notice can be less strict than
the threshold stated in
R. v. Find
,
2001 SCC 32
:

[105]    Where a fact is dispositive of an issue in
dispute, a judge may only take judicial notice where: (1) the fact is
clearly uncontroversial and beyond reasonable dispute
;
or (2) it is capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to
readily accessible and accurate sources:
R. v. Find
,
2001 SCC
32
at para.
48
;
Le
at paras. 84–85.

[106]    The standard for taking judicial notice is less strict
in circumstances where an extrinsic fact is relied upon solely for context.
When a fact will “… merely paint the background to a specific issue … courts
will usually take judicial notice … and the threshold is lower”:
Le
at
para. 85.

[107]

Importantly,
where an extrinsic fact falls in the middle of the spectrum, in that it
may not be dispositive, but does more than “merely paint the background”, a
trial judge must not take judicial notice of it without first asking
whether that fact “… would be accepted by reasonable people who have taken
the trouble to inform themselves on the topic as not being the subject of
reasonable dispute
for the particular purpose for which it is to be
used
…”:
Spence
at para. 65, italics in the
original.

[
42
]

Here, I do not consider the Society’s four statements in their
entirety to be clearly uncontroversial and beyond
reasonable dispute; however, the Society submits that the public protests over
logging in TFL 46 are relevant context for the Petition.

[
43
]

For that contextual reason, the Court can take judicial notice that in
the last four years, logging operations in TFL 46 have
been the subject of public protests disrupting logging operations, and there
has been associated litigation with numerous cases including injunction
applications and contempt proceedings; see, as just two of many examples:
Teal Forest Products Ltd. v. Rainforest Flying Squad
,

2021 BCSC 605
, leave to appeal ref’d
2021 BCCA 353
, relating to an injunction
prohibiting road blockades and other activities intended to obstruct Teal
Cedar’s logging activities; and
Teal Forest Products Ltd. v. Rainforest Flying
Squad
,
2023 BCSC 1406
, regarding criminal contempt proceedings against a
person found to have breached the injunction order
.

VI.

Standing

[
44
]

Neither of the two applicants, AGC and AGBC, challenge the Society’s
standing to bring the Petition; nevertheless, I will briefly review the basic
principles of public interest standing. The Society’s standing was not a contested
issue at the hearing of the applications. I recognize that the Society would
have made more substantive submissions on standing had the other parties
challenged the Society on that issue.

[
45
]

In
Canada
(Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence
Society
,
2012
SCC
45
[
Downtown Eastside
]
at paras.
7 and 36
the Supreme Court of Canada stated the three factors to
be considered by a court in exercising the discretion to grant public interest
standing:
(1) whether there is a
serious justiciable issue
raised; (2) whether the
plaintiff has a real stake or a genuine interest in it; and (3) whether, in all
the circumstances, the proposed suit is a reasonable and effective way to bring
the issue before the courts; and the plaintiff seeking public interest standing
must persuade the court that these factors, applied purposively and flexibly,
favour granting standing. T
he
factors are interrelated considerations to be weighed cumulatively, not
individually, and in light of their purposes. See also
Council of Canadians
with Disabilities v. British Columbia (Attorney General)
,
2020 BCCA 241
at paras.
67–101
.

[
46
]

The Society submits that the issue before the Court is a serious issue
because logging of old growth forests in TFL 46 has been the subject of significant
controversy and litigation.

[
47
]

However, public protests and controversy regarding logging of old
growth forests do not, without something more, necessarily raise a serious
justiciable issue.

[
48
]

The Society’s submissions refer to what it describes as a critical
issue being whether the province can issue permits allowing for the
contravention of the federal
MBR
. As will be discussed in more detail below
in the analysis section, I question whether
the Petition and the declaration sought by the Society directly
address that issue, and whether the Petition is a reasonable and effective way
to bring that issue and the issues as plead in the Petition before this Court.

[
49
]

Regarding the second factor of standing
regarding the nature of the Society’s interest: “th
is
factor reflects the concern for conserving scarce judicial resources and the
need to screen out the mere busybody,” requiring an examination of the
plaintiff’s reputation, continuing interest, and link with the claim, thus
assessing the plaintiff’s “engagement”:
see
Downtown Eastside
at para.
43
.

[
50
]

Here, Teal Cedar’s response to the Petition states that the Society
was incorporated on January 23, 2023, relatively recently, and Teal Cedar
states there is no evidence regarding the Society’s members, activities, or
funding, leaving limited evidence on the Society’s engagement other than the
Society’s stated purpose being to preserve the remaining old growth forest in
TFL 46. That focus, and the Society having brought the Petition, provide some
support for the Society’s standing by virtue of its engagement and interest in
old growth forests and logging in TFL 46.

[
51
]

Despite my reservations about the way in which the Society has plead
the issue, in assessing standing it is clear that the Court is to take a
flexible, discretionary and purposive approach to public interest standing:
Downtown
Eastside
at para.
44
.

[
52
]

Considering the three factors in light of that approach, and
considering that the respondents AGC and AGBC have not objected to the Society’s
standing to bring the Petition, I find that for the purpose of these two
applications to strike the Petition there is a
serious justiciable issue raised by the Society, and the
Society has a genuine interest in it.

[
53
]

For the reasons that follow, while I am not
convinced the Petition is a reasonable and effective way to bring the issue
before the Court, I conclude that cumulatively considering the three factors weighs
in favour of the public interest standing of the Society.

VII.

Analysis

Rule 9-5(1)(a): does the Petition
disclose a reasonable claim?

[
54
]

The AGC and AGBC apply to strike the Petition on the Rule 9-5(1)(a)
ground that the Petition does not disclose a reasonable claim.

[
55
]

The AGC and AGBC’s submissions do not take issue with the four
factors from the
Interfor
case: the court’s jurisdiction; the dispute is
real; the party raising the issue has a genuine interest; and the responding
party has an interest in opposing the declaration being sought.

[
56
]

The AGC and AGBC’s focus is on the practical utility, or lack thereof,
of the declaration being sought.

[
57
]

A first issue, and it is first because it is immediately apparent
from a first reading of the declaration sought, is the wording of the declaration,
which is that the
MBR
prohibit the “indiscriminate destruction of Marbled
Murrelet nests by the logging of old growth trees in TFL 46”.

[
58
]

The factual basis of the Petition does not allege
indiscriminate destruction

of nests by logging. The factual basis of the Petition states that Teal Cedar
harvests timber, builds roads and engaged in related forestry activity in TFL
46 “pursuant to provincial authorization” and pursuant to a “Management Plan”,
with consequent loss of nests.

[
59
]

I recognize the word
destruction
is likely used by the
Society as a synonym of the word
destroy
in s. 5 of the
MBR

prohibitions, but the word destruction when combined with the word
indiscriminate
,
creates a more loaded phrase than a simple reference to the specific words used
in s. 5 of the
MBR
.

[
60
]

The word
indiscriminate
is defined in The Concise Oxford
Dictionary as “done or acting at random or without careful judgment”.

[
61
]

Read in the light of the definition of indiscriminate, the proposed
declaration is vague, or as the AGBC submits – abstract – as disassociated from
the material facts in the Petition relating to the provincial authorization and
management plan.

[
62
]

Also apparent on a first reading of the declaration, is that the
Society’s use of the term
indiscriminate destruction
has an appearance
of rhetoric. The use of that loaded phrase, without the Petition seeking any form
of enforceable relief, also has the appearance of having been intentionally worded
to enlist the Court to make a boldly worded declaration in an attempt to apply pressure
on the federal and provincial governments on the issue of logging in TFL 46.

[
63
]

A declaration is not a mere
observation or comment by the court on how it views a situation, rather it is a
binding statement by the court establishing a right, power, duty or status:
Pereira

at para.
16
.

[
64
]

I agree with Teal Cedar’s pleadings in its response to the Petition
that the Society seeks an abstract interpretation of the
MBR
; the phrase
“indiscriminate destruction” is imprecise, and would introduce ambiguity into
the
MBR
and confuse rather than guide those subject to the
MBR
.

[
65
]

As a result, the wording of the declaration suggests an effort by the
Society to have this Court make a comment or statement beyond
establishing a right, power,
duty or status.

[
66
]

In addition to the vague or abstract wording of the declaration, the
Petition itself has internal inconsistencies which provide a challenge for
a clear understanding of the nature of the
claims advanced
.

[
67
]

The purpose of Rule 9-5(1)(a) is to ensure that
the parties and the court have a clear understanding of the nature of the
claims advanced
.
A clear
understanding of the claims will allow the parties to efficiently litigate the
issues and will allow the court to make considered and judicious findings on
those issues
: see
Simon
quoting
Gill
.

[
68
]

The inconsistencies in the Petition and the declaration are apparent
in the Petition’s references to the facts, the
MBR
, the stated narrow question,
and the broader declaration sought by the Society, as follows.

[
69
]

The Petition sets out the material facts, very simply summarized
here as allegations that logging old growth trees in TFL 46 results in a loss
of nests and nesting opportunities for marbled murrelets.

[
70
]

The legal basis of the Petition then refers to s. 12 of the
MBR

which provides that the federal Minister may issue a permit for a variety of
scientific, commercial or public interest reasons, and the federal government “also
publishes ‘Avoidance Guidelines’ in respect to the incidental tak[ing] of
migratory birds in Canada and the destruction of their habitat.”

[
71
]

The ministerial permit is referred to in s. 5(1) of the
MBR

as one of the qualifications to the prohibitions in that section, that is: “A
person must not engage in any of the following actions,
unless
they have a permit that authorizes them to do so or they are authorized by
these Regulations to do so
…”.

[
72
]

The Petition then states: “Whether or not a permit has been granted
in respect to old growth logging in TFL 46, or whether the logging is in
compliance with the Avoidance Guidelines is irrelevant to this application. The
question before the court is not whether the logging is lawful, but the narrow
question of whether such logging is exempt from the prohibitions contained in
the
MBR
.”

[
73
]

I understand the issue the Society seeks to address in the Petition
is based on the Society’s submission that logging trees in TFL 46 damages or
destroys marbled murrelet nests, an activity prohibited by s. 5(1) of the
MBR
;
and, if that logging activity does not fall within one or more of the
exceptions in s. 5(2) of the
MBR
, the Society submits that the provincial
state action in issuing permits for that activity is contrary to the federally
enacted
MBR
and consequently unlawful.

[
74
]

However, the Petition:

1.

ignores or considers irrelevant a portion of the enactment to be
interpreted:
unless they have a permit that authorizes them to do so or they
are authorized by these Regulations to do so;

2.

asserts a narrow question focussing on only one aspect of s. 5
of the enactment (the exceptions in s. 5(2));

3.

then asserts that if the logging does not fall
within the exceptions, the result from that narrow premise is the wider
declaration that the
MBR
prohibit the indiscriminate destruction of
marbled murrelet nests by the logging of old growth trees in TFL 46.

[
75
]

The declaration is effectively the Society seeking what it has just
stated is not the question, that is, whether the logging is lawful. That
broader question cannot be answered based only on an analysis of the exemptions
in s. 5(2), there is the s. 5 reference to a permit, and the
Avoidance Guidelines, and decisions relating to the provincial authorization to
Teal Cedar to conduct logging operations in TFL 46.

[
76
]

As stated in
Rizzo & Rizzo Shoes Ltd. (Re)
, [1998]
1 S.C.R. 27,
1998 CanLII 837
at para.
21
; and
Bell ExpressVu Limited Partnership v. Rex
,
2002
SCC 42
at para.
26
, the
proper approach to statutory interpretation is Elmer Driedger’s “Modern
Approach”: “[T]he words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in
their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act,
the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.”

[
77
]

As a result, the narrow basis upon which the Society seeks an
interpretation of the
MBR
makes it difficult for the parties and the
Court to have a
clear
understanding
of the
claims to allow the parties to efficiently litigate the issues and allow the
Court to make considered and judicious findings on those issues.

[
78
]

The next question is whether there is any practical utility to the
declaration sought.

[
79
]

The Society submits that it is an established role for declarations
to delineate boundaries between the application of federal and provincial law;
however,  the issues noted above regarding the vague declaration sought and the
inconsistences in the Petition do not appear to enable a delineation of such
boundaries here.

[
80
]

An assessment of the practical utility of a declaration necessarily
looks at the effect of the requested remedy on the parties’ rights, that is, if
it will settle a live controversy:
West Moberly
at para. 310.

[
81
]

Here, as noted above, I agree with the AGBC that what the petitioner
is seeking is an abstract legal opinion, and I agree with the AGC and the AGBC
that the declaration sought will have no practical utility because the wording
of the declaration sought by the Society will not settle any controversy associated
with the logging in TFL 46.

[
82
]

A declaration that the
MBR
prohibits “indiscriminate
destruction of marbled murrelet nests” is vague and no remedy is sought. The
Petitioner’s assertion that the Petition relates to a long-standing and very
public conflict over the logging of old-growth trees, without seeking a remedy
beyond the declaration sought, suggests that the petitioner is seeking to
pressure the respondent governments by the political or moral suasion of the
declaration, emphasized by the loaded wording:
indiscriminate destruction
.
Moral suasion is discussed with reference to
Lyn/Gor Developments
below

in the analysis section on Rule 9-5(1)(b).

[
83
]

A further point about the practical utility of the relief sought by
the Society, including the absence of a pleading for a remedy, is the Society’s
reliance on Rule 2-1(2)(c) for raising the issue by way of petition.

[
84
]

Rule 2-1(2)(c) provides that a person must file a petition where the
sole or principal question at issue is alleged to be one of construction of an
enactment.

[
85
]

In
Walters v. Agricultural Land Commission
,
2016 BCSC 1618
,
the Court considered whether a petition was the appropriate manner of
proceeding. The Court referred to the predecessor of Rule 2-1(2)(c) considered
in
Three Stars Investments Ltd. v. Narod Developments Ltd
,
1981 CanLII
696
(BCSC), 33 B.C.L.R. 164 (BCSC), where the Court held at para. 10 that
a petition under Rule 10(1)(b) (now Rule 2-1(2)(c)) is inappropriate where:

1.

Serious questions of law or fact are raised;

2.

A decision will not end the matter, but requires
further proceedings to be pursued;

3.

The application involves not the interpretation but
enforcement of a contract.

[
86
]

On the second point about ending the matter, in
Walters

the Court refers to
Three Stars
at para. 8 quoting extensively from

Lewis v. Green
,
(1905) 2 Ch. 340 at page 343
regarding other Courts’
considerations of whether petitions or similar originating applications are
appropriate, specifically on the issue of construction, as follows:

Now, under those circumstances, the applicant persists
in asking me to determine these questions of construction. In my opinion I
ought not to do so. It seems to me that under such circumstances as those under
which this summons was issued, Order LIV. A is not the appropriate mode of
procedure.

…
The result will be this: the Court may, after
considerable litigation … come ultimately to the decision that on the questions
of construction raised by this summons the applicant is right.
Well, what then? No relief can be given on that
. There
are other points which have to be decided.
They can only be decided by
bringing an action, and in that action it may turn out that, notwithstanding
the applicant is right on the questions of construction, he is ultimately found
to be wrong.

…

[The procedure] is only intended to enable the Court
to decide questions of construction where the decision of those
questions,
whichever way it may go
,
will settle the
litigation between the parties.
It is not intended that questions of
construction which, if they are decided in one way only will settle the dispute
between the parties, should come up for decision on an originating summons. It
would be most inconvenient to resort to the order in a case where it is quite
uncertain what may be the ultimate decision on the point of construction, and
where if the decision is in one way it involves further litigation.

[Italics
emphasis in original; underline emphasis added.]

[
87
]

The result in the
Three Stars
case was that the court held
that the petition was inappropriate because a declaratory judgment regarding
the construction of the contract would not settle all issues between the
parties. The parties would still have to go on to trial to enforce whatever
contract was found.

[
88
]

Here, similarly, granting the declaration sought by the Society would
not settle all the issues between the parties because of the narrow question
and the vague declaration sought. Even if the declaration was made, the same
questions from
Lewis
arise: “Well, what then? No relief can be given on
that. There are other points which have to be decided.”

[
89
]

Considering all of the above, I conclude that there is no reasonable
prospect of success of the Society in this Court granting the declaratory
relief sought by the Society.
The
pleadings of the Petition do not provide the parties and the Court with a clear
understanding of the nature of the claim advanced.
The
pleadings of the Petition do not support the declaratory relief sought as a
binding statement of the court in establishing a right, power, duty or status.
Given the wording of the declaration, if granted it would likely cause more
uncertainty regarding the
MBR
. As a result, the declaration sought by
the Society will not have a practical effect, it will not settle a live
controversy, and it will not resolve an extant legal dispute.

[
90
]

I agree with the AGBC’s conclusion that even if the pleaded facts
are true, it is plain and obvious that this Court will not grant the relief
sought.

[
91
]

In
International Taoist Church of Canada v. Ching
Chung Taoist Association of Hong Kong Limited
,
2011 BCCA 149
at para.
28
,

Justice Low stated
that when there is an attack on a pleading as showing no reasonable claim or
defence, the court is well advised to first consider whether the pleading can
be preserved by amendment.

[
92
]

Here, I will consider the possibility of an amendment to the
Petition below following my analysis on the other
two
grounds of Rule 9-5(1): (b) and
(d).

Rule 9-5(1)(b): is the Petition unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious?

[
93
]

Regarding Rule 9-5(1)(b),
the AGC raises the question of what the wording of the Petition seeks, submitting
that the Society seeks to enlist Canada in the petitioner’s effort to halt
logging on TFL, in that sense submitting that an order for
mandamus

against Canada would fall within the jurisdiction of the Federal Court.

[
94
]

As quoted from
Willow
, above,
a
pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the
plaintiff's cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known in law,
where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no
useful purpose and would be a waste of the court's time and public resources.

[
95
]

Here, in light of my
findings in the preceding section of these reasons regarding ground (a) of Rule
9-5(1) that the declaration sought by the Society will have no practical
utility and will not settle any live controversy, it follows that the pleadings
will serve no useful purpose and for that reason I find that the Petition is
unnecessary.

[
96
]

Further, I also agree with
the AGC that the petitioner’s framing of the amended petition in naming as the only
respondents the AGC and AGBC, and in seeking a declaration worded with the
vague and loaded phrase “indiscriminate destruction”, suggests that the
intended purpose of the Petition is to attempt to enlist this Court to pressure
the respondents on the issue of logging in TFL 46.

[
97
]

Regarding the AGC’s
submissions that the declaration sought by the petitioner is a disguised
mandamus

remedy, the absence of a remedy in the Petition raises some doubt about this
Court’s jurisdiction to hear the issue in relation to the AGC, jurisdiction
being the first of the four pre-requisites in
Interfor
as the basis for
the Court exercising its discretion to grant declaratory relief.

[
98
]

Boloh 1(a)
and
Lyn/Gor Developments
assist in this
analysis.

[
99
]

In
Boloh 1(a)
, the
Federal Court of Appeal set aside “declarations” granted by the Federal Court
on the basis that they were disguised mandatory orders or disguised
mandamus

remedies requiring the Government of Canada to take specific actions to assist
Canadian citizens detained in Syria.

[
100
]

The Federal Court of Appeal
found that the essential character and real essence of the remedy the Federal
Court had awarded was the imposition of mandatory obligations on the Government
of Canada, something akin to
mandamus
, not declarations which are
supposed to be declarations of rights held by those seeking them:
Boloh 1(a)

at paras. 60–62.

[
101
]

I distinguish that case
because here the declaration sought by the Society does not seek to directly
impose mandatory obligations on the AGC, it appears to be more indirect, which
is more consistent with the court’s comments in
Lyn/Gor Developments
.

[
102
]

In
Lyn/Gor Developments
,
the applicant, who contracted to construct a new federal building in New
Brunswick, sought a declaratory order against the federal government that the
applicant had a right to resolve disputes relating to the construction contract
by way of the dispute resolution clause in the contract. The applicant
submitted that the declaration depended simply on an interpretation of the
contract.

[
103
]

The Court of Queen’s Bench of
New Brunswick concluded that there was a substantial dispute of fact, not just
a question of interpretation, and the Court had no jurisdiction to impose a
mandatory order on the federal Crown by way of injunction or specific
performance, referring to s. 22 of the
Crown Liability and Proceedings
Act
,
R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7
:
Lyn/Gor Developments
at para. 13

[
104
]

The applicant conceded that
the government would not be required to act as a matter of law, but suggested that
“such a declaratory order would exercise considerable moral suasion on the
government to act in accordance with the declaration.” The Court concluded by
stating that that is not the intended purpose of the legislation and it was not
a judicial role that the court was inclined to undertake.

[
105
]

Similarly, here, the Society

naming only the AGC and AGBC as respondents, and wording
the declaration with the phrase
indiscriminate destruction
, suggests an
intended purpose of the
Petition to enlist the Court in exercising moral
suasion on the provincial and federal governments. As stated in the
Lyn/Gor
Developments
case, this is not a judicial role that this Court is inclined
to undertake.

[
106
]

The AGC also points to the Federal Court proceedings in the
Western
Canada Wilderness Committee
case as an example of a more
appropriate means for raising the issue the petitioner
seeks to raise before this Court
.

[
107
]

That proceeding was the subject of a recent decision by the Chief
Justice of the Federal Court: see
Western Canada Wilderness Committee
v. Canada (Environment and Climate Change)
,
2024 FC 167
.

[
108
]

The decision is useful for
this analysis because it deals with the same issue for which the Society
expresses concern: protection of the marbled murrelet and its habitat on
southern Vancouver Island.

[
109
]

The
Western Canada
Wilderness Committee
proceeding
is
an application for judicial review by the two
petitioners pursuant to
s. 18.1
of the
FCA
.

[
110
]

Section 17
of the
FCA
provides that the
Federal Court has concurrent original jurisdiction in all cases in which relief
is claimed against the federal Crown.

[
111
]

Section
18
of the
FCA
provides that the Federal Court has
exclusive

original jurisdiction to
issue an injunction, writ of

certiorari
, writ of prohibition,
writ of

mandamus

or
writ of
quo warranto
,
or grant
declaratory relief
,
against
any federal board, commission or other
tribunal.

[
112
]

The subject of the
Western
Canada Wilderness Committee
judicial review was a
decision of the Minister of Environment and Climate Change (the “Minister”) to issue
a protection statement pursuant to
SARA
for habitat to which the
MBCA

applies for migratory birds listed under
SARA
, including the habit of
the marbled murrelet.

[
113
]

The Chief Justice’s decision was that the
Minister’s decision was unreasonably narrow in its determination that the
critical habitat, contemplated by the relevant provision of
SARA
is
confined to nests. In the result, the Chief Justice set aside the protection
statement and remitted it to the Minister for redetermination in accordance
with the Chief Justice’s reasons.

[
114
]

Another example of how the
issue the Society seeks to raise before this Court has been addressed is
Western
Canada Wilderness Committee v. British Columbia (Ministry of Forests, South
Island Forest District)
,
2003 BCCA 403
, an appeal of a decision of a chambers
judge dismissing the petition for judicial review of the decision of a provincial
Ministry of Forests District Manager (“DM”).

[
115
]

The chambers judge upheld
the DM’s decision that the logging
company’s Forest Development Plan (“FDP”) for one of four
proposed cutblocks met the requirements of
s. 41(1)
of the
Forest Practices Code of
British Columbia Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 159 [
Code
], solely as it relates to the adequate
management and conservation of the spotted owl as a forest resource. For the
other three cutblocks the DM decided that the FDP did not meet the requirements
of the
Code
.

[
116
]

These two
Western Canada Wilderness Committee
decisions provide examples of how parties with public
interest standing interested in the management and conservation of bird species
and their habitat in the forests of British Columbia have focussed on the decisions
by provincial and federal decision-makers in the specific context of logging
operations in the forests of southern Vancouver Island, to address specific
issues relating to habitat for birds: one case requiring the federal government
to reconsider its protection statement for critical habitat for the marbled
murrelet, and the second case relating to spotted owl habitat.

[
117
]

For the reasons above, I
conclude that the Petition would serve no useful purpose, and it has the
appearance of an improper purpose. As a result, I find that the whole Petition is
unnecessary and should be struck out, subject to my consideration of the
possibility of an amendment, below.

Rule
9-5(1)(d): is the Petition otherwise an abuse of the process of the court?

[
118
]

Rule 9-5(1)(d) provides that
the Court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that it is otherwise an
abuse of the process of the court.

[
119
]

The AGC submits that the Petition
is an abuse of process for asking this Court to take the role of prosecutor,
not the appropriate prosecution service, by seeking a declaration from this
Court that the logging of old growth trees in TFL 46 is prohibited by
MBR
, s. 5(1).

[
120
]

The AGC submits that the Petition is effectively
asking this Court to make a finding that the logging is unlawful, which would constitute
an offence under s. 13(1) of the
MBCA
, and where in a criminal
prosecution there could be potentially significant fines on conviction on
indictment or summary conviction, subject to a defence of due diligence.

[
121
]

The AGC cites
R. v. Syncrude Canada Ltd.
,

2010 ABPC 229
, as an example of a prosecution of a company under the
MBCA
.
In that case several hundred waterfowl died after being trapped in bitumen on
the surface of the company’s settling basin. The Provincial Court of Alberta found
that the alleged offences were strict liability offences in which the accused
will be found guilty if the Crown proves the accused committed the prohibited act
beyond a reasonable doubt. A statutory due diligence defence is available to
the accused in s. 13.18 of the
MBCA
if the accused can prove on a
balance of probabilities the company exercised due diligence to prevent the
commission of the offence.

[
122
]

By contrast, to emphasize
the point that a declaration such as that sought by the petitioner here is an
abuse of process, the AGC cites
Reece v. Edmonton (City)
,
2010 ABQB 538
,
aff’d
2011 ABCA 238
.

[
123
]

In that case, the applicants
– an individual and two organizations interested in the treatment of animals –
sought a declaration that the City of Edmonton was in violation of a section of
the
Animal Protection Act
, R.S.A. 2000, C. A-41 [
APA
] in relation
to the health and care of an elephant in a zoo.

[
124
]

The Court of Queen’s Bench
of Alberta agreed with the City’s position that the declaration sought by the
applicants was a statement of the Court that the City was acting contrary to
the
APA
, which created an offence and imposed penalties. The Court found
that a declaration was not appropriate, as the applicants were attempting to
act as private prosecutors, which was an abuse of the criminal process of the
courts.

[
125
]

The Court of Appeal of Alberta dismissed the
appeal, and in so doing commented on applications to strike an action for abuse
of process, as follows:

[15]      An application to strike an
action for abuse of process raises a pure question of law about the legal
legitimacy of the pleadings.

…

[20]      The cases on abuse of process have
tended to fall into a number of categories … One such category is where
proceedings are used to enforce or engage punitive penal statutes, other than
by charging the party allegedly responsible with the applicable offence. Such
proceedings are generally found to be an abuse of process. Sometimes the court
reaches that result by finding that the applicant has no standing to apply for
the requested relief.

[
126
]

The Court of Appeal of Alberta also provided
reasons why courts are reluctant to grant such a declaration, as follows:

[29]      … For one thing, the burden of proof in civil
proceedings is on a balance of probabilities, whereas the burden of proof in
penal regulatory proceedings is proof beyond a reasonable doubt:
F.H.
v. McDougall
,
2008 SCC 53
,
[2008] 3 S.C.R. 41
at paras.
40
,
49;
R. v. Lobbins (#2)
,
1940 CanLII 408 (AB CA)
,
[1940] 3
W.W.R. 301
,
74 C.C.C. 274 (Alta. S.C., App. Div.)
.
The presumption of
innocence in penal proceedings is lost or undermined in a declaratory action.
In penal proceedings the respondent has the right to remain silent, and has no
obligation to call evidence; in civil proceedings the respondent is often
compelled to call evidence, or disclose its defence. Other evidentiary and
procedural protections of the criminal process are lost
:
Gouriet
at
pp. 481, 487-9, 498-9;
Ed DeWolfe
at para. 25;
Manitoba
Naturalists Society
at paras. 24-6;
R. v. Richard
,
1996
CanLII 185 (SCC)
,
[1996] 3 S.C.R. 525
at para.
19
;
R. v.
Wigglesworth
,
1987 CanLII 41 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 541
at p. 554
.
Where a person is charged with a penal offence the protections of ss. 7
and 11 of the
Charter
are engaged, and they should not be
undermined by changing the form of the procedure.

[30]
Civil proceedings of this nature can also have the
effect of undermining the jurisdiction of the criminal courts
:
Ed
DeWolfe Trucking
. In this case, if the respondent City had been charged
with an offence under the Act, the trial would have been in the Provincial
Court. The proceedings brought by the appellants had the effect of transferring
the issue to the Court of Queen’s Bench.

[31]
Civil proceedings of this sort also
undermine the authority of the Attorney General in the enforcement of the law
:
Gouriet
at
pp. 477, 489-90, 506, 511-12, 521. If any complainant swore an information
that the respondent City was in breach of the Act, the Attorney General
would have the option of taking over the prosecution, or of staying the
proceedings. Seeking a declaration takes the matter out of the hands of the
Attorney General, and bypasses the penal sanctions contemplated by the
Act
.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
127
]

See also
R. v. Shore Disposal
Ltd
.,
1976 CanLII 1235 (NS CA)
, [1976] N.S.J. No. 404,
16 N.S.R. (2d) 538 (C.A.), in which the Court of Appeal for Nova Scotia stated
at para. 24 that a
declaration that the defendant has committed an
offence is gratuitous and almost impertinent advice to the summary conviction
court, and may also be in effect an injunction, disregard of which may visit
upon the defendant penalties harsher far then the legislature ordained.

[
128
]

The Society submits that the Court of Appeal has held that in the
face of a significant public controversy it is appropriate for the Court to
interpret a statute to provide clarification of the powers of the province,
citing
Association for the Protection of Fur-Bearing Animals v. British
Columbia (Minister of Environment and Climate Change Strategy),

2018 BCCA
240
.

[
129
]

In my view, that case is more accurately cited,
and supportive of the AGC’s submissions, for the Court of Appeal’s caution that
proceedings regarding contraventions of a statute are normally determined
through
quasi criminal
proceedings.

[
130
]

Although the Court of Appeal was willing to give
some guidance about the interpretation of the statute in the specific
circumstances of that case, in so doing the Court stated that it is not
appropriate to inquire into the specific circumstances of the matter that
brought the case before the Court, in that case the killing of a bear cub, as
follows:

[18]

… My main concerns with this proceeding are
more substantive. At the outset of the hearing of this application,
the
Court expressed concerns as to the appropriateness of a judicial review
proceeding to determine whether Officer Kneller had contravened the
Wildlife
Act
. Contraventions of the statute are normally determined through
quasi
criminal
proceedings, which afford those charged strong procedural protections,
and require proof of all elements on a criminal standard
. Counsel for the
appellant conceded that judicial review proceedings should not be used to
circumvent the protections afforded to persons accused of offences. He said,
however, that the interpretation of the
Wildlife Act
is an
important issue, and that the current proceedings were an appropriate vehicle
to settle certain questions with respect to the statute.

[19]      While I accept that it is
possible

for this Court, in this appeal, to give some guidance with respect to the
interpretation of the
Wildlife Act
, I do not accept that it would
be appropriate to treat these proceedings as an inquiry into the specific
conduct of Officer Kneller or the specific circumstances of the killing of the
bear cub. This is not a prosecution for the commission of a Provincial offence.

[Emphasis
added.]

[
131
]

These statements of the Court of Appeal on the appropriateness of
the proceedings, and the interpretation of the statute, apply equally well to
the case at bar.

[
132
]

Here, I agree with the AGC that the declaration sought by the
Society would be in effect a statement by this Court that the logging
operations in TFL 46 constitute an offence under the
MBR
, and as such
the Petition is an abuse of process of this Court.

Amend the Petition?

[
133
]

As noted above,
when
there is an attack on a pleading as showing no reasonable claim or defence, the
court is well advised to first consider whether the pleading can be preserved
by amendment:
International Taoist Church
at para. 28.

[
134
]

In
Jones v. Bank of Nova Scotia
,
2018
BCCA 381
, the Court of Appeal discussed the discretion to permit an amendment
to pleadings, as follows:

[35]      ...
The exercise of that discretion may require consideration, including the degree
to which the pleadings are deficient, of the extent to which the deficiencies
may be addressed by an obvious or straightforward amendment, the apparent merit
of the claim that may be made out with amendment and the prejudice that may be
incurred by dismissing the claim.
The exercise of
that discretion requires consideration of the factors set out in Rule 1‑3:

(1)

The object of these
Supreme Court Civil Rules
is to secure the
just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every proceeding on its merits.

(2)

Securing the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of a
proceeding on its merits includes, so far as is practicable, conducting the
proceeding in ways that are proportionate to

(a) the amount involved in
the proceeding,

(b) the importance of the
issues in dispute, and

(c) the complexity of the
proceeding.

[
135
]

Here, in
analysing the pleadings on grounds a, b and d of Rule 9-5(1) above, I have
described the inconsistency and lack of clarity of the pleadings in the
Petition, and the vagueness and ambiguity of the declaration. As a result, the
pleadings are deficient to a high degree and I do not consider the deficiencies
to be capable of being addressed, or of straightforward amendment.

[
136
]

Although
there is prejudice to the Society in striking the Petition, it does not
preclude the Society from proceeding with a more appropriate procedure.

[
137
]

Regarding
consideration of the factors in Rule 1-3, I do not consider these factors to
weigh in favour of permitting an amendment to the pleadings when considered in
the context of the deficiencies referred to above. There is no monetary value plead
in the Petition, but any disruption in logging in TFL 46 would be expected to
have a serious economic impact on affected parties. The issues raised by the
Petition are of some significance to the parties, with a potentially broader
impact. The proceeding has some complexity, but given the deficiency of the
pleadings, an amendment to the existing pleadings would not assist in determination
of the proceeding in a just, speedy and inexpensive determination on its merits.

[
138
]

As a result,
given
the significant concerns with these particular pleadings, it is not
foreseeable how the Society might further amend its Petition to address the
concerns set out in these reasons.

VIII.

Conclusion and Disposition

[
139
]

For all of these reasons,
having found that the Petition discloses no reasonable claim, is unnecessary
and an abuse of the Court pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a), (b) and (d), I order that
the petitioner Society’s amended petition filed April 24, 2023 is struck without
leave to amend.

[
140
]

The AGC
and
AGBC as the
successful parties on the two application are entitled to their costs from the
Society.

“Jones J.”
